newsitem.title: USA: Aetna eyes Asia as middle class booms.
newsitem.headline: Aetna eyes Asia as middle class booms.

text.p: U.S. insurance giant Aetna Inc. said Monday its burgeoning Asian business will be increasingly driven by an exploding middle class hungry for basic life insurance and healthcare services.

The company expects its Asia-Pacific revenues and earnings to enjoy double-digit growth for the next few years, the head of Aetna International's Southeast Asian operations, James E. Simon, told Reuters in an interview.
"In Asia Pacific, revenues and earnings growth have been continually spectacular for the last four or five years," Simon said.

Asia-Pacific represents about 45 percent of Aetna International's total earnings. In the first quarter of 1997, Aetna International represented about 15 percent of Aetna Inc.'s total, $186.8 million operating earnings before unusual items.
The company is expected to report second-quarter earnings on August 5. Aetna International is one of the company's three businesses, along with Aetna U.S. Healthcare and Aetna Retirement Services.
Aetna hopes to enter Thailand in January 1998, and is finalizing negotiations with an undisclosed joint-venture partner, Simon said.
"In Thailand we plan to sell individual life and some group employee benefits-type products," he said.
Aetna's other regional businesses include Hong Kong, Malaysia, New Zealand, Taiwan, Indonesia and the Philippines.
The 144-year-old company has more than 1.2 million policyholders in the Asia-Pacific, and $2 billion in assets under management.
The insurer is actively seeking out opportunities in China, India, and Vietnam, Simon said.

Aetna's representative office in China has applied for a license to write business in Shanghai. "We've been working on the entry for five years," Simon said. "We're very encouraged, (and) we are hopeful that the license is imminent."
He said prospects in India are still somewhat foggy, due to uncertainties over the government's pace of insurance liberalization.
"India's attraction is basically that they've got the world's biggest middle class -- about 250 million people."
Simon said Malaysia, a country of 20 million where Aetna is the third-biggest life insurer, is typical of the company's Asian markets.
"You have people who, 15 years ago, were working on rubber plantations, and today they are making cellular telephones for Motorola." Aetna entered Malaysia 10 years ago.
"We feel our opportunity is to start penetrating these emerging markets as the middle class grows," he said.
In addition to life insurance, the company is bullish on healthcare services, which represents 30 percent of Aetna's business overseas, Simon said.
"We believe that healthcare is going to be a global market. The challenge as you expand... is to sort out where each local environment is in the evolution of healthcare."
In sizing up new markets, Aetna emphasizes political stability and sound industry regulation, he said.
Aetna's international strategy will keep its focus on emerging markets "which have hit the take-off points," Aetna President and Chief Executive Richard Huber told Reuters.
He cited Taiwan, Indonesia, and Malaysia -- in addition to Latin American countries like Brazil -- as promising markets.

"These are countries where the growth in the middle class has hit an inflection point, the point where the demand for basic insurance products tends to grow exponentially," Huber said. ((--Hartford newsroom, (860) 727-0224))
